problem: Language-conditioned navigation policies lack large language- and action-annotated navigation datasets. Zero-shot foundation-model pipelines (CoW, OWL-v2 + depth, OpenFMNav) are slow on edge compute and brittle to noisy or complex instructions.
motivation: Robots need to reach arbitrary objects that people describe in natural language. Abundant action-free egocentric video (robot logs, YouTube tours, human walking) exists but has no language or action labels. Foundation models for segmentation, vision-language, depth and navigation can label such video automatically. This would let a small, fast policy learn grounded language-conditioned navigation.
key_idea: Automatically label action-free egocentric videos with object-goal language prompts and counterfactual robot actions using SAM, CogVLM, GPT-3.5, monocular depth and NoMaD, then train a small end-to-end language-conditioned navigation policy on the result.
insight: Diverse in-the-wild video is what makes the policy generalize. In the data ablation, the YouTube Tour data keeps improving pose error beyond 100K frames while the indoor robot and human-walking data saturate. On the real robot, training with only the indoor robot data gives 0.65 success, 20% YT + 43.5% HW gives 0.85, and the full data gives 0.89. Robustness to noisy prompts and speed come from the compact policy: 0.054 s on a Jetson Orin, versus 0.22 s for the fastest baseline, CoW. The collision-avoidance term J_col distilled from NoMaD raises success with obstacles from 0.13 to 0.60, at a cost in success without obstacles (0.89 to 0.77).
method: Language annotation: Segment Anything gives masks and boxes; each crop is described by CogVLM, and GPT-3.5-turbo filters low-confidence detections and generates several diverse 'Go to X' prompts per object.

Goal pose estimation: Metric3D (narrow FOV) or Depth360 (wide FOV) monocular depth is projected to a point cloud, masked with the SAM mask, and the median gives the 3D object pose, which is projected to a 2D goal.
Counterfactual action labels: NoMaD, fine-tuned to accept cropped object images as goals, generates collision-avoiding trajectories toward each object crop, used as supervision.

Policy architecture: a frozen CLIP text encoder feeds a ResNet-FiLM visual encoder trained from scratch on the current image. Past-frame features from EfficientNet-B0 go through a Transformer and MLP to output 24 (v, ω) velocity pairs, integrated by a differentiable kinematic model.

Objective: J = J_pose (final virtual pose vs object pose) + ε·J_col (distill NoMaD trajectory, masked when the object is within 1 m) + J_smooth (velocity differences). J_col is added by pre-training without it and then fine-tuning.
Data: 31 h indoor robot data (GS2, GS4, SACSoN), 82.5 h YouTube tours, 15.7 h human walking with a fisheye camera (11 cities, 3 countries), sampled at 2 FPS for the video data.
Long-distance extension: topological memory with OWL-v2 node scoring and ViNT navigate to the selected node, then switch to LeLaN for the last mile.

setting.backbone: Small policy (frozen CLIP ViT-B32 text encoder + ResNet-FiLM + EfficientNet-B0 + Transformer/MLP) trained from scratch, with labels from SAM, CogVLM, GPT-3.5-turbo, Metric3D/Depth360 and NoMaD
setting.training_data: Automatically labeled action-free video: 31 h indoor robot data (111,570 images), 82.5 h YouTube tours (593,727 images), 15.7 h human walking (113,277 images); about 20M prompts in total. No human labels.
setting.observation: Monocular RGB (front fisheye of a RICOH Theta S; also narrow FOV and spherical cameras), current frame only (L=0) at evaluation
setting.action_space: Predicted sequences of continuous linear/angular velocities (24 steps), executed receding-horizon with the first command

results: LeLaN reaches 0.89 total success over 150 real-robot trials, against 0.67 for the strongest baseline (OWL-v2 + Zoedepth) and 0.58 for CoW. It is especially strong on noisy prompts (0.88) and dynamic objects (0.83 vs at most 0.33), and runs 4x faster than the fastest baseline. It also transfers to a quadruped and to different cameras.
limitations: Cannot disambiguate multiple copies of the same object using spatial language (e.g. 'leftmost door').

Collision avoidance is still weak (0.60 with obstacles, and it lowers success without obstacles to 0.77); the method is last-mile only, so the target must be visible at the start, and long-distance use needs an external topological memory.
Labels depend on noisy monocular depth and open-source VLM descriptions; evaluation is small-scale, on a single robot, with success measured by reaching within 0.2 m.
